claim: Telling people after learning that a test is coming raises overnight retention after sleep in the founding study (word pairs 117.3 vs 105.2 percent, p=0.014; card locations 98.8 vs 73.1; finger tapping 131.1 vs 117.0), with no gain after wake. Re-verified against the paper text.
agent_test: Two agent arms at equal tokens: lessons tagged 'will be needed' vs untagged at write time, same store size; measure reuse accuracy on later tasks.

claim: The sleep x expectancy interaction is fragile: Wilhelm's was p=0.05 with post hoc exclusion of suspicious subjects, Wamsley 2016 (maze/motor, N about 100) found equal benefit after sleep and wake (interaction p=.38, .33), Reverberi 2020 (N=38, no wake group) found no effect.
agent_test: Do not build a rule that depends on a sleep-specific relevance advantage; treat as a prior only.

claim: Telling people which items matter improves memory for those items regardless of sleep (main effect of expectancy: Wamsley F(1,71)=7.35 p=.008; relevance in Barner 2023 F(1,54)=8.78 p=.005; Kurdziel 2025: remember instruction beat emotion).
agent_test: Cheap test: a written 'this will be reused' flag on a lesson improves its later retrieval or use vs no flag, at equal tokens.

claim: Sleep selectively supporting relevant over irrelevant items was reproduced only weakly: Van Dongen 2012 (N=50, relevance x group F=13.19) positive; Barner 2023 (28 sleep, 28 wake) had main effects but interaction p=0.12; only a planned 1-week contrast was significant.
agent_test: Treat 'relevance gates consolidation' as plausible, not proven; hedge design choices.

claim: What happens to relevant vs irrelevant items during wake is inconsistent across studies (Wilhelm: expectancy changes nothing; Van Dongen: relevant lost more, -5.0 vs -3.3, p=0.005; Wamsley: expectancy helped in wake as much as in sleep).
agent_test: None; reason not to assume a wake baseline when comparing agent arms.

claim: Reward is the best-supported relevance cue for sleep selection: about half of sleep x reward tests are positive (Fischer and Born 2009 N=76; Tamaki 2020), with nulls (Tucker 2011) and a reversal under time-pressure reward (Stamm 2014).
agent_test: Test value tags from observed outcome (reward) vs tags from an LLM rating, at equal tokens.

claim: Pramipexole (D2 agonist) before sleep removed the high-over-low reward advantage while the encoding-strength advantage stayed; the review favours a tag set at learning over dopamine acting only during sleep.
agent_test: Tag lessons at write time with an outcome-based value rather than computing value only at consolidation.

claim: Directed forgetting: a nap boosted Remember-cued words but not Forget-cued words (Saletin 2011, N=46, interaction F=6.17 p=0.004; fast spindles r=0.66) but replications are partial or null (Scullin 2017 older adults, Rauchs; Kurdziel 2025 sleep had no effect).
agent_test: Test explicit 'forget' tags on lessons: do dropped lessons cut interference without losing needed ones?

claim: Emotional memory is not preferentially kept by sleep overall: a meta-analysis of 31 studies (36 datasets) found no overall effect, only moderated by free recall, initial-learning control and design.
agent_test: Do not use emotion or salience tags as a retention signal without a test.

claim: Weak traces are replayed more and gain more from sleep, so relevance does not simply track strength; in rats sleep replay rose with laps run and fell with track familiarity (p=0.0002, 4 rats). In humans, a 2021 task found the weak-trace sleep gain only under easy retrieval (Petzka: weak d=1.19, strong d=0.41 ns; with interference strong d=1.70), and a 2025 study (N=90) found sleep kept weak and strong pairs alike while wake lost mostly the weak ones.
agent_test: Compare keep-strong vs keep-weak-but-relevant retention rules in an agent store.

claim: Learning-time EEG theta (3-8 Hz) tags items that survive a nap (N=31, sleep advantage d=0.45; classifier separates sleep-kept items), supporting tagging at encoding.
agent_test: Analog: record write-time features (surprise, effort) and check they predict later use.

claim: Boundary: with 640 word pairs sleep gave neither benefit nor extra forgetting (N=78, p=0.27; equivalence rules out harm beyond d=-0.20), so sleep does not erase when load is high.
agent_test: Store-size sweep: does pruning help only past a load threshold? Compare with ZenBrain stress results.

claim: In LLM agent memory, blind (query-agnostic) multi-factor value beats uniform, recency and single-factor retention (LongMemEval-S, 479 cases, keep 30%: 0.770 vs 0.657 vs 0.368); learned weight on goal relevance is 0.00; goal relevance wins only when it sees the future query (0.979 vs 0.286 blind). Re-verified.
agent_test: Replicate on our own task logs with held-out future tasks; proxy is gold-evidence retention, not answer accuracy.

claim: Utility-based deletion (remove a record after at least n retrievals when the mean utility of those retrievals is low) improves some agents and hurts others, depending on judge and agent. Strict evaluator, none -> history: EHRAgent 38.67 -> 42.06, CIC-IoT 85.40 -> 89.60, AgentDriver 51.00 -> 51.81, RegAgent 70.95 -> 67.65 (memory 2938 -> 949). Coarse evaluator: EHRAgent +7.6, CIC-IoT +4.1, AgentDriver -2.9, RegAgent -2.3. Row pairing inferred from memory sizes. Add-all causes error propagation.
agent_test: A/B: add-all vs success-gated add vs history-based deletion at equal token budget.

claim: Utility- and relevance-weighted forgetting cuts memory size at similar or better accuracy in several 2026 preprints (FadeMem 82.1 vs 78.4 critical facts at 55 percent storage; OBLIVION 68-73 percent token cut; SF-AMS multi-hop +9.65 F1), but most are author-built and unreplicated.
agent_test: Compare score-based prune vs no prune at equal tokens on our tasks.

claim: Forgetting can hurt: under high load, ablations that looked costless at moderate load became critical (ZenBrain: 9 of 15, quality down up to 93.7 percent), and ConsolidationBench FORGET destroyed 74 percent of load-bearing clusters at least once with precision at base rate (0.319 vs 0.333).
agent_test: Forget-by-default is risky: prefer demotion (suppress from view, keep source) as in RD-Forget and OBLIVION.

claim: Separating stored source from a per-query view (suppress rather than delete) is a viable design: RD-Forget three-suite means 66.6 to 86.7 across four models; OBLIVION treats forgetting as lowered accessibility. Removing RD-Forget's rescue (historical eligibility) step cost 3.5 to 9 points (91.86 -> 88.37, 93.59 -> 91.03, 74.00 -> 65.00), and in ConsolidationBench rollback that restores source experiences lifted success from 0.0 to 1.0 (5/5 seeds). OBLIVION matched or slightly beat flat retrieval (90.60 vs 89.00 on LongMemEval-S) mainly saving tokens. No study runs suppress against hard delete head to head.
agent_test: Soft-forget vs hard-delete at equal tokens.

claim: Precomputing offline for likely future queries cuts test-time compute about 5x at equal accuracy and adds up to +13 percent (GSM) and +18 percent (AIME); the gain shrinks when the query is less predictable from context. Re-verified. Predictability binned in five quantiles on GSM: the gap grows with predictability. On SWE-Features the gain exists only at low test-time budgets; standard test-time scaling wins at higher budgets.
agent_test: Pre-write likely-reuse notes between tasks; test at equal total tokens (offline plus test time).

claim: Production-style memory (Mem0-style, SimpleMem-style) retains but gives zero cross-level transfer in ConsolidationBench; only fixed-level or learned abstraction policies transfer (synthetic benchmark).
agent_test: Check whether our lessons are stored as abstractions that transfer to new tasks.

claim: No study found tests whether an LLM relevance proxy (importance rating, retrieval count) predicts actual future use; in LLM work relevance is a proxy of recency, access count, LLM rating or query match.
agent_test: Direct test: log whether each lesson is used later and regress on proxies.

claim: A rough pool of five independent test-expectancy x sleep interaction tests (Wilhelm 2011, two Ashton and Cairney 2021 experiments, Wamsley 2016 maze, Barner 2023), all signs set positive, gives r about 0.10 with 95 percent CI 0.01 to 0.18; the two online replications (N=162, N=124) give BF01 of 2.5 to 4.0 for no interaction. This is an own back-calculation, not a published meta-analysis, and no meta-analysis exists.
agent_test: Treat sleep-specific relevance selection as small or absent; keep relevance tagging only for what the agent retrieves, not for what an offline pass erases.

claim: In human tests a relevance or expectancy instruction raises retention in wake as well as in sleep (Wamsley: F(1,71)=7.35), so the replicated effect is an attention or encoding effect, not a sleep-triage effect.
agent_test: Apply the relevance tag at write time (what to encode carefully), not as an offline selection pass.

claim: Explicit in-context 'forget' or 'ignore' instructions do not reduce proactive interference in LLMs: the per-key forget prompt gave under 10 points at 100 updates and was negative for gpt-4.1-mini; errors clustered at the instruction position. Only a fake Q&A reset helped, with declining benefit. (Synthetic key-value streams, five models.)
agent_test: Remove dropped lessons from the context or use a hard task boundary; do not rely on a 'drop' note in the same prompt.

claim: Soft forgetting is safer than hard deletion under budget pressure: a learned forget policy destroyed 74 percent of load-bearing clusters at least once at chance precision; rollback that restored sources recovered success from 0.0 to 1.0; adding a hindsight-regret signal raised forgetting precision to 0.93 but nearly switched the gate off (0.61 forgets per seed vs 30).
agent_test: Keep an archive of dropped lessons with a rescue path; log regret (a dropped item needed later) as the training signal for the drop rule.

claim: Whether pruning pays depends on store size and judge: the only human boundary is 640 pairs (no benefit, no harm); in agents deletion gains appear at stores of about 900 to 1200 records with a strict judge (EHRAgent, CIC-IoT, AgentDriver) and a 2938-record synthetic agent lost 3.3 points, so no clean threshold has been measured.
agent_test: Sweep store size (50, 200, 1000 lessons) with keep-all, recency and utility-gated deletion at equal tokens before enabling deletion.

claim: No tested write-time signal (surprise, effort, theta analogue) has been shown to predict later reuse of an agent lesson; the closest are outcome-based (retrieval-utility history, hindsight regret), which exist only after use. Search for new direct tests was cut off by quota limits.
agent_test: Log write-time features and later reuse per lesson; fit a simple model and compare against recency and access count.
